text: This lesson teaches a repeatable method for finding bugs in code you've never seen before -- exactly what a whiteboard security round is actually testing.

Five steps, every time. Read the function's purpose first. List every state variable it touches, in order. List every external call and exactly where it sits relative to state changes. Check every arithmetic operation for overflow or underflow. And check every state-changing function for who can actually call it.

Here the external call happens before the balance is decremented. A malicious contract's receive function can call withdraw again mid-call, and since the balance hasn't updated yet, the check still passes -- repeatedly. The fix: update state before the external call.

This subtraction sits inside an unchecked block, which disables Solidity's default underflow protection. If amount exceeds the real staked balance, it wraps to a huge number instead of reverting, and the function still transfers tokens the caller never had.

This function changes where protocol fees get sent, with no access control at all. Any address can call it and redirect every future fee payment to themselves. The fix is a simple ownership or role check.
